中国
国常会部署深化拓展"人工智能+"行动，要求从我国产业体系完备、应用场景丰富、工程化能力强的实际出发，以落地应用牵引技术创新，夯实发展底座、加强技术攻关和算法创新、促进算电协同、增加高质量数据供给，并以实体经济为重点强化供需衔接。会议还讨论并原则通过价格法修正草案，明确不正当价格行为认定标准，提出依法依规治理低价无序竞争、持续规范平台经济领域价格竞争行为。
商务部、科技部拟对40项技术实施出口管制，涉及人工智能、生物医药、光伏三个领域，其中拟禁止出口14项、限制出口26项。人工智能领域涵盖大模型、智能体、算力集群、信息处理等23项技术，已通过开源、发表论文进入公共领域的技术不纳入管理；光伏领域涵盖多晶硅、硅片、电池制造12项技术。自公告发布之日起，相关技术出口前须在商务部业务系统统一平台登记。商务部称此次修订不针对任何特定国家或实体。
央行规范银行间债券市场债券发行行为，就《银行间债券市场债券发行管理规则》公开征求意见。《规则》共二十八条，明确禁止发行人认购或变相认购自己发行的债券，禁止干预投资者认购决策或以返费干扰定价；禁止承销机构低价承销、事先承诺投标价格；禁止投资者虚假投标、蓄意大量申报并撤销。簿记场所须全程记录询价、定价决策信息并形成不可篡改记录。
商务部回应欧盟拟动用"反胁迫"工具，称中欧按遵守世贸组织规则、基于事实和非歧视三项原则就混动汽车达成的谅解是对等互利的，所谓"欧方施压奏效"的说法毫无依据。商务部表示，欧方不能幻想以施压换取好处，更不要低估中方维护自身利益的决心和能力，敦促欧方与中方相向而行。
四部门组织30余家重点汽车生产企业座谈，要求加强汽车产品创新设计和研发测试验证管理，全面加强测试验证、及时消除安全隐患，如实宣传产品创新设计的使用边界、限制条件和研发测试验证情况，不得作虚假、夸大或引人误解的宣传，不得诱导驾驶人忽视安全驾驶责任。工信部表示将加快推进标准制修订，对重点企业持续开展监督检查并向社会公开曝光。
长鑫科技前三季度净利润超1300亿元，预计归母净利润1310亿元至1325亿元，较上年同期亏损52.80亿元大幅扭亏；营业收入预计2650亿元至2700亿元，同比增长逾七倍。公司将业绩改善归因于AI算力需求带动全球DRAM景气度提升、产品供不应求价格大幅上涨。董事长朱一明提议回购10亿至20亿元股份。
长安汽车管理层大变阵，朱华荣继续担任中国长安汽车集团党委书记、董事长，不再兼任上市公司重庆长安汽车董事长，集团总经理赵非接任上市公司董事长，原常务执行副总裁叶沛出任总裁。此次调整距离朱华荣获选连任上市公司董事长不足一个月。今年前三季度上市公司长安汽车累计销量169.27万辆，同比下降18.07%。
北汽蓝谷拟为北汽新能源增资不超过21.38亿元，其中上市公司出资不超过10亿元、北汽集团出资不超过6.38亿元，另通过公开挂牌引入不超过5亿元外部投资，主要用于补充日常经营流动资金。今年前三季度北汽新能源累计销量16.34万辆、同比增长46.52%，上半年营收115.97亿元、归母净亏损19.38亿元。
理想汽车芯片子公司完成首轮融资，上海马赫心科技签署首轮股权融资协议，认购总额16.25亿元，理想汽车出资10亿元、外部投资方合计6.25亿元，若追加认购权悉数行使，投后估值最高达171亿元。融资将用于芯片及域控制器研发与商业化，推进面向外部客户的产品供应。马赫M100采用5nm车规级工艺、单颗算力1280 TOPS，已搭载于新一代理想量产车型。
海外
美芯片股八连跌，市值蒸发约2万亿美元，费城半导体指数连续第八个交易日下跌，创2008年金融危机以来最长连跌纪录，本周累跌11.4%，八个交易日累计跌逾13%。若按各股较52周高点跌幅计算，整个板块损失市值约达4万亿美元，但该指数年内仍累涨约60%。美光本周跌14.6%，存储芯片指数累跌17.6%；CoreWeave周五再跌11.9%，本周累计跌超25%。
- 费城半导体连跌八个交易日，黄仁勋："这一切终将过去"：英伟达CEO在柏林表示市场动荡终将过去，AI变革才刚刚开始。
- 巴克莱：AI交易"最佳阶段"已过，芯片股暴跌是仓位出清而非基本面崩塌：高盛预测五大超大规模公司明年资本支出约1.2万亿美元。
沃什曼谷发言偏鸽，市场押注10月按兵不动，美联储主席沃什在IMF年会对话中重申致力于价格稳定，但明确表示"我不会预判会议结果"，市场对10月27日至28日会议加息的概率预期从约27%骤降至15%以下。高盛首席经济学家Jan Hatzius团队指出，结合其他官员表态，沃什此番讲话进一步表明美联储将在10月按兵不动，下次加息预计在12月落地。
- 美联储主席沃什：AI是我一生中最深远的经济变革，10月和12月议息会议至关重要：沃什称9月加息以来全球经济走势大体符合预期，并宣布放弃"前瞻指引"策略。

美国众议院两党议员提出议案阻击俄罗斯柴油协议，众议院外交事务委员会民主党首席委员Gregory Meeks提出的《禁止腐败的俄罗斯石油交易法》拟撤销财政部海外资产控制办公室已发放的第135号等一般许可，禁止未来继续发放豁免，并要求总统在法案生效30天内对参与俄罗斯油气开采、炼制及海上运输的主体实施制裁。议案消息公布后，美股午盘之初WTI原油一度接近100.90美元，布伦特原油一度逼近109.60美元。
美国拟提供最多1700万桶战略储备原油，能源部16日提出新一轮原油交换计划，交付时间为11月至次年1月，投标方须在2028年至2029年间归还原油并额外交付至少12.5%的溢价。该计划属于今年3月承诺提供1.72亿桶原油的一部分。美国战略石油储备规模目前为1.862亿桶，为1982年10月以来最低水平。今年6月类似交换因溢价过高，最终仅约50万桶获企业借用。
- IEA加速释放1亿桶原油储备，并承诺优先释放"2000万桶柴油"：成员国已释放3.3亿桶，剩余1亿桶系补足3月承诺缺口，美欧在是否追加释放上存在分歧。

美财政部一级交易商调查未释放削减发债信号，美债收益率走高、10年期重上5.12%。在征询一级交易商意见的调查中，美国财政部问到长期国债的回购计划、如何提高回购效率、短债发行时点、经济与融资前景，却没把问题直接指向减少长债供给。部分投资者原本期待，财政部会借此次问卷更明确地暗示正考虑缩减长债标售规模，甚至停止发行20年期国债。11月4日财政部公布的再融资公告成为下一观察点。花旗预计，届时会将20年和30年期美债标售规模各削减30亿美元，认为本次调查显示财政部在考虑减发长债。
美国2026财年赤字扩大至1.99万亿美元，较上一财年增长约12%，支出增长约6%至7.4万亿美元，收入增长约3%至5.4万亿美元。净利息支出增加814亿美元至1.05万亿美元，首次突破万亿美元门槛；全年总利息支出达1.360万亿美元，预计将于2028年底前超过社会保障支出。财政部将关税退款列为赤字扩大因素之一，2025年减税法案则令企业所得税收入下降逾700亿美元。
8月海外资金重返美债市场，美国财政部国际资本流动报告显示，8月海外投资者净买入美国国债1089亿美元，总持仓升至9.3317万亿美元。英国持仓史上首次突破万亿美元至1.0095万亿美元，加拿大增持383亿美元居首。日本持仓减少356亿美元至1.0683万亿美元、连续四个月下降；中国大陆持仓减少273亿美元至5907亿美元，连续两个月创2008年8月以来新低。
软银考虑收购美国最大安保公司，据彭博社报道，软银集团正就收购Allied Universal展开初步研究，可能给后者带来最高180亿美元的股权估值，叠加约120亿美元公开交易债务，交易总价值或接近300亿美元。消息传出后，软银ADR单日暴跌近10%至每份14.72美元。孙正义已将安保服务定位为检验旗下投资组合公司机器人技术的关键试验场。
Meta发布8160亿参数开放权重模型，Muse Spark Open支持100万Token上下文窗口，实际激活参数420亿，主攻编程与智能体任务，采用Muse Model License授权。Meta称其为迄今美国能力最强的开放权重模型，但能力不及本周一推出的闭源Muse Wonder系列。Meta同时与苹果合作，让模型可在两台Mac Studio上运行。
- 苹果和Meta和好了，是AI逼的：此前苹果曾因Meta智能体读取Mac私人消息调整系统规则，两周后双方转为合作。
苹果首款折叠屏手机iPhone Duo开启预购，10月16日20时开启预售后苹果官网和App被挤崩，10月23日首发日到店取货迅速售罄，邮寄下单发货时间已排到明年1月下旬。该机256GB版本售价15999元，1TB版本21499元。得物App显示多个版本预售成交价突破2万元，1TB黑色版本接近2.9万元，比发售价高出7143元。
- iPhone Duo预购倒计时，京东预约超200万，代抢费炒到888元：京东渠道首批商品要求消费者签收时当面激活，闲鱼代抢服务报价300元至1000元不等。
三季度全球智能手机出货量暴跌22%，IDC初步数据显示当季出货量降至2.553亿部，同比萎缩22.0%，创有纪录以来季度同比最大降幅。存储芯片成本较去年上涨约350%，前五大品牌出货量同比全部下滑，OPPO、vivo降幅均超30%。IDC预计市场增长将持续受限至2027年，复苏至少要推迟到2028年。同期中国大陆智能手机出货量5930万台，同比下滑12%。
CoreWeave三位创始人IPO后套现33亿美元，据彭博报道，联合创始人Michael Intrator、Brian Venturo和Brann McBee自2025年3月上市以来累计出售价值33亿美元股票，其中2026年一年套现24亿美元。同期公司五年期信用违约互换利差一度升至1194.5个基点，隐含五年内违约概率超过60%。McBee近40%的个人财富目前以现金及等价物形式持有。
- 危险的信号？CoreWeave三位创始人IPO后套现33亿美元：Intrator自年初以来出售逾9.07亿美元，为过去两个季度美国公司五大内部卖家之一。
观点精选
德银：AI将把企业切割成采纳者与出局者两类。这份20页报告援引前谷歌CEO施密特的"旧金山共识"，认为超级智能将于2030年前后到来，企业间几乎不存在中间地带。报告援引Epoch数据称，过去三年AI几乎每季度降价一半，相当于每年价格缩减约13倍，算力走完同等降幅耗费了六十年。德银认为传统投资组合管理的三大基石——分散化、以历史波动率衡量风险、下跌时买入——在双峰世界中均可能失效。
桥水：本轮利率上行是供给驱动的资本市场再定价。报告指出，利率上行更多反映经济增长超预期韧性与资产供给扩张，而非单纯能源冲击。超大规模云服务商已用尽自身自由现金流，正由向市场提供资金转为从市场获取资金；现代重商主义推动军费与产业政策投入增加，资产净供给规模已接近过去半个世纪高点，需要价格敏感型投资者承接的比例越来越高。
美银Hartnett：未来数周仍倾向规避风险。美银报告显示，美国股票基金单周吸引390亿美元流入，今年年化流入规模有望达6360亿美元历史新高，科技股以107亿美元流入居首；美国国债连续第16周录得资金流入，创2024年8月以来最长纪录。但Hartnett团队认为，实际收益率上升、AI及银行股价格走势叠加中期选举不确定性，仍支持防御立场。
高盛：对冲基金已清空2025年以来AI净买入，逼空燃料充足。数据显示对冲基金连续五个交易日净卖出全球AI股票，2025年以来的净买入头寸被彻底清除，净配置比例从6月峰值31.7%降至26.1%，多空比从4.34降至3.27、处于过去一年第7百分位。全球股票净流量达负2.1个标准差，多头平仓与空头卖出之比约3比1，指向主动降低敞口而非做空押注。
德银：黄金量化抛压接近绝对耗尽。金属研究主管Daniel Ghali指出，量化基金风险平价组合的去杠杆规模已达2010年以来完整样本的第90百分位，CTA基金被迫回补约20%的黄金净空头头寸，白银、铂金、钯金分别需增加7%、13%、15%。模拟显示几乎所有价格情景下算法系统目前均偏向买入黄金，但金价需升至约4370美元才能触发下一轮大规模程序化买入。
穆迪分析：伊朗战争已给美国家庭带来近2000美元成本。首席经济学家Mark Zandi估算，自2月28日美以对伊朗发动打击以来，综合经济负担约2650亿美元，其中能源与交通成本约1100美元、加息导致的借贷成本约540美元、军事支出分摊约360美元。这笔成本已吞噬美国普通家庭过去八个月收入增幅的约一半。白宫迅速驳斥该测算，并质疑Zandi的立场与过往预测记录。
摩根士丹利：AI资本开支暗藏"租赁账单"，2027年投资额上调至1.5万亿美元。该行指出，除自建数据中心外，算力租赁承诺正成为科技巨头表外的重要支出来源，这部分隐性负债使市场对真实资本开支强度的评估偏低。在折旧年限与租赁合同期限错配的情况下，未来的利润压力可能比当前盈利指引所显示的更晚、也更集中地显现。
高盛：韩股估值已跌至极低水平，坚守KOSPI 12000点目标。亚太首席股票策略师Tim Moe维持12个月目标位不变，较目前5700点约有110%上涨空间。KOSPI此前连续七个交易日收跌、最大累计跌幅约20%。高盛认为抛压源于三星电子、SK海力士回购买盘退出叠加外资集中减持，外资卖出中约80%至87%集中于这两只存储权重股，属流动性驱动而非需求前景重定价。
澳新数据中心IPO连环折戟，成为全球数据中心债务危机的引线。英伟达与黑石支持的澳大利亚数据中心运营商Firmus撤回原将成为澳洲史上第二大IPO的上市计划，其寻求的估值达440亿澳元，为三个月前融资估值的两倍，且上市后计划举借最高300亿美元债务。数日后AirTrunk亦取消在新加坡上市REIT的计划。CoreWeave CEO将公司股价下跌部分归咎于此。
今日关注
双11大促进入首个周末，京东、淘天、飞猪等平台活动持续放量，飞猪双11开售4小时活动商品累计销量接近100万件，超200个商家成交额较去年翻倍增长。
美联储自10月17日起进入10月27日至28日议息会议前的静默期，决策者暂停公开发声；沃什16日在曼谷的表态是本轮会议前最后一次公开讲话。
IMF与世界银行年会期间，G20财长与央行行长会议继续举行，全球增长、通胀、利率与政府债务仍是核心议题。
风险提示及免责条款
市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

items.title: 全球股市小幅反弹，韩股收涨2%，SK海力士涨逾4%，美元小幅下跌

items.text:
美联储主席沃什拒绝就进一步加息发出明确信号，令市场从本周通胀数据冲击中企稳。全球股市普遍走高，美元承压回落。


沃什周四在曼谷出席国际货币基金组织活动时，将人工智能描述为其有生之年美国及全球经济最具深远影响的变革，并称其在中期构成正向供给冲击。他未就货币政策路径作出任何前瞻性表态，仅重申美联储将致力于实现价格稳定，并表示"不会预判会议结果"。


沃什的表态迅速带动市场重新定价。交易员将本月美联储加息的押注概率从周四的逾25%降至15%。美元指数下跌0.1%，此前一个交易日已累计下挫0.3%，创逾一个月最大单日跌幅。亚太股市和欧洲股市随之走高，美股期货亦小幅上涨。


DBS Bank宏观策略师Wei Liang Chang指出，"市场对沃什重申AI将在中期提振生产率的判断感到宽慰，这有助于缓和通胀预期，并压低连续加息的担忧。"


欧洲斯托克50指数涨0.4%，德国DAX指数涨0.5%，法国CAC 40指数涨0.3%，英国富时100指数则小幅下跌0.4%。


韩国首尔综指收涨2%，报5668.05点，日经225指数收涨1.4%，报65324.29点；日本东证指数收涨1.7%，报4066点。


美国10年期国债收益率上涨3个基点，至5.09%


日本10年期收益率上涨4.5个基点，至2.935%


澳大利亚10年期收益率上涨2个基点，至5.23%


美元指数下跌0.1%


黄金价格基本持平于每盎司4172美元。


布伦特原油下跌0.7%，报每桶105.20美元

加息预期松动，风险资产获喘息空间

Saxo Markets首席投资策略师Charu Chanana表示，"沃什拒绝承诺再次加息，导致部分美联储加息押注被平仓。在强劲通胀数据公布后，他表示'不会预判会议结果'，这一措辞对美元构成压制。"


美联储于9月上调利率25个基点，为2023年以来首次加息，并获全部19名政策委员一致支持，多数委员亦预计年内可能再度加息。此后数周，多位官员重申可能需要进一步紧缩，但强调有足够时间收集经济数据再行决策。


芯片股止跌，亚欧市场普遍上涨

在沃什讲话之前，全球股市已因芯片股抛售潮趋缓而率先走高。亚洲市场方面，三星电子和SK Hynix均涨逾4%，带动韩国首尔综指收涨2%，报5668.05点，从周四跌至4月以来最低收盘价的低谷中反弹。日经225指数收涨1.4%，报65324.29点；日本东证指数收涨1.7%，报4066点。

欧洲市场开盘亦整体偏强，欧洲斯托克50指数涨0.4%，德国DAX指数涨0.5%，法国CAC 40指数涨0.3%，英国富时100指数则小幅下跌0.4%。


值得关注的是，印度尼西亚股市盘中一度暴跌逾11%，创1998年1月以来最大跌幅，原因是MSCI宣布将印尼从新兴市场指数中剔除，印尼盾亦小幅走低。

反弹持续性存疑，科技板块集中风险犹存

黄金价格基本持平于每盎司4172美元。布伦特原油下跌0.7%，报每桶105.20美元，油价高企持续为通胀预期提供支撑——中东冲突爆发以来，油价一直是美国通胀顽固维持高位的重要推手。

此轮股市反弹能否延续，在一定程度上取决于涨势能否从主导今年大部分升幅的科技重仓股扩散至更广泛的板块。本周的剧烈波动暴露了市场过度依赖AI概念股的风险，更广泛的板块参与将有助于降低这种集中度风险。


东洋证券策略师Ryuta Otsuka表示，"目前看来是一次技术性反弹，整体市场情绪有所平复。"他同时提醒，下周随着投资者继续追踪财报数据并"寻底"，市场波动率可能仍维持相对高位。

items.title: 华尔街腹背受敌：AI抛售潮蔓延至债市，110美元油价再添一把火
items.summary:
AI基础设施融资风险与能源价格骤升同步爆发，令华尔街本周承受双重冲击。


纳斯达克100指数本周累跌5.5%，创下2025年4月关税动荡以来最大单周跌幅；半导体板块八连跌，为2008年以来最长连跌纪录，区间跌幅约16%。云计算服务商CoreWeave成为市场焦点——其部分债券收益率周四一度突破15%，信用风险攀升至通
items.text:
AI基础设施融资风险与能源价格骤升同步爆发，令华尔街本周承受双重冲击。


纳斯达克100指数本周累跌5.5%，创下2025年4月关税动荡以来最大单周跌幅；半导体板块八连跌，为2008年以来最长连跌纪录，区间跌幅约16%。云计算服务商CoreWeave成为市场焦点——其部分债券收益率周四一度突破15%，信用风险攀升至通常预示财务困境的水平，股价周五单日再跌12%，较年内高点累计腰斩逾50%。

与此同时，布伦特原油收于每桶约110美元附近，WTI原油单日涨幅达3.8%，油价骤升加剧通胀顾虑，推动10年期美债收益率升至5.097%，令债市的避险逻辑受到侵蚀。

本周市场的核心转变在于：AI交易的主要矛盾已从算力需求增长，转向融资成本、资本开支回报与企业盈利能力。两大风险——AI泡沫估值松动与能源驱动的通胀压力——在同一时间窗口集中释放，对股票、债券与信用市场形成联动压制。

AI债务风险浮出水面，CoreWeave成引爆点

CoreWeave的信用恶化是本轮抛售的直接导火索。这家新兴云计算服务商依靠大规模举债建设AI数据中心基础设施，其债务融资模式在本周遭到市场的集中审视。CoreWeave部分债券收益率周四一度突破15%，其违约概率被市场定价至约60%，信用风险已进入困境区间。


市场的担忧并不局限于CoreWeave一家。Siebert Financial首席投资官Mark Malek表示，新兴云服务商融资渠道收紧，可能成为整个科技行业供应链中"令人非常不安的一道坎"。"现在我们看到，融资本身将成为一种稀缺资源，并将影响供应链，"他说。


Montis Financial首席投资官Dennis Follmer——旗下管理约14亿美元资产——同样对超大规模云厂商的负债状况保持警惕。"市场的很多担忧来自于超大规模云厂商的借贷规模——他们在需要举债之前已经消耗了大量现金流，"Follmer表示，"我确实认为这在未来会带来一些麻烦。"


JPMorgan策略师指出，与7月份的抛售相比，当前AI交易的修复基础更为薄弱——零售买盘偏弱、可供轧空的空头头寸规模更小，企业回购的支撑力度也相对有限。

芯片与存储板块遭集中减仓

此轮抛售从云计算延伸至整个AI产业链上游。费城半导体指数八连跌，为2008年全球金融危机以来最长跌势；存储概念指数单周下跌6.28%。SK海力士ADR单日跌超6.5%，美光科技跌超5.6%，闪迪跌超6.8%，光通信公司Coherent跌逾7%。

追踪DRAM内存芯片的ETF本周跌幅达19%，创自今年4月成立以来最大单周跌幅，并已连续八周录得资金净流出。韩国综合股价指数本周重挫14%，为2008年金融危机以来最大单周跌幅，较夏季峰值累计下挫逾37%。


据彭博银行美国10月份基金经理调查显示，将"做多全球半导体"列为最拥挤交易的受访者比例已从7月份的82%降至45%——尽管降幅显著，拥挤程度仍居首位。JonesTrading首席市场策略师Michael O'Rourke直言：

"市场对AI公司的估值已计入泡沫溢价，这个泡沫正开始收缩。"


油价骤升撕裂避险逻辑，债市双重承压

在能源市场，布伦特原油本周升至每桶约110美元，为今年5月以来最高水平；WTI原油单日涨幅达3.8%，报每桶101.71美元，连续七日上涨。美国两党议员联合提出法案，拟阻止特朗普政府与莫斯科达成的俄罗斯柴油入市协议，地缘政治因素进一步支撑油价。


油价上涨在债市引发连锁反应。此前，即便连续两份高于预期的通胀数据也未能阻止投资者在股市下跌时涌入国债避险；但随着油价骤升，通胀顾虑重燃，10年期美债收益率升至5.097%，扭转了此前三连降走势，长端债券的避险属性在周五受到明显侵蚀。

美联储主席沃什在曼谷国际货币基金组织活动上拒绝对10月利率会议前景提供任何指引，令市场进一步缺乏政策方向支撑。尽管如此，以TLT ETF衡量的长期国债整体仍录得年内表现较强的一周。Follmer表示，其团队已开始削减久期风险，以巨灾债券部分替代传统固收持仓。

分歧加剧：减仓与抄底并行

尽管恐慌情绪升温，市场并未出现无差别的风险出清。投资级信用利差仍维持在近五年区间的偏紧端，部分ETF投资者选择逢低买入。


Cathie Wood旗下ARK Investment Management趁此机会增持了CoreWeave和Cerebras Systems的股票。Wood将当前市场对CoreWeave借贷成本的焦虑，比作早年Coinbase债券承压时期——彼时加密货币交易所随后受益于行业的整体成长。


Truist Advisory Services首席投资官Keith Lerner同样维持对科技板块的超配立场，认为大部分利空信息已反映在股价中，部分估值已接近历史区间低端。


市场的真正考验即将到来。未来数周，科技巨头将陆续披露财报，届时投资者将检验AI相关营收能否与持续攀升的资本开支相匹配。与此同时，美国中期选举临近，为跨资产定价增添额外的不确定性。正如Mark Malek所言："这是任何一个行业走向成熟必经的阶段。"

市场的担忧并不局限于CoreWeave一家。Siebert Financial首席投资官Mark Malek表示，新兴云服务商融资渠道收紧，可能成为整个科技行业供应链中"令人非常不安的一道坎"。"现在我们看到，融资本身将成为一种稀缺资源，并将影响供应链，"他说。
Montis Financial首席投资官Dennis Follmer——旗下管理约14亿美元资产——同样对超大规模云厂商的负债状况保持警惕。"市场的很多担忧来自于超大规模云厂商的借贷规模——他们在需要举债之前已经消耗了大量现金流，"Follmer表示，"我确实认为这在未来会带来一些麻烦。"
JPMorgan策略师指出，与7月份的抛售相比，当前AI交易的修复基础更为薄弱——零售买盘偏弱、可供轧空的空头头寸规模更小，企业回购的支撑力度也相对有限。
芯片与存储板块遭集中减仓
此轮抛售从云计算延伸至整个AI产业链上游。费城半导体指数八连跌，为2008年全球金融危机以来最长跌势；存储概念指数单周下跌6.28%。SK海力士ADR单日跌超6.5%，美光科技跌超5.6%，闪迪跌超6.8%，光通信公司Coherent跌逾7%。
追踪DRAM内存芯片的ETF本周跌幅达19%，创自今年4月成立以来最大单周跌幅，并已连续八周录得资金净流出。韩国综合股价指数本周重挫14%，为2008年金融危机以来最大单周跌幅，较夏季峰值累计下挫逾37%。
据彭博银行美国10月份基金经理调查显示，将"做多全球半导体"列为最拥挤交易的受访者比例已从7月份的82%降至45%——尽管降幅显著，拥挤程度仍居首位。JonesTrading首席市场策略师Michael O'Rourke直言：
"市场对AI公司的估值已计入泡沫溢价，这个泡沫正开始收缩。"
油价骤升撕裂避险逻辑，债市双重承压
在能源市场，布伦特原油本周升至每桶约110美元，为今年5月以来最高水平；WTI原油单日涨幅达3.8%，报每桶101.71美元，连续七日上涨。美国两党议员联合提出法案，拟阻止特朗普政府与莫斯科达成的俄罗斯柴油入市协议，地缘政治因素进一步支撑油价。
油价上涨在债市引发连锁反应。此前，即便连续两份高于预期的通胀数据也未能阻止投资者在股市下跌时涌入国债避险；但随着油价骤升，通胀顾虑重燃，10年期美债收益率升至5.097%，扭转了此前三连降走势，长端债券的避险属性在周五受到明显侵蚀。
美联储主席沃什在曼谷国际货币基金组织活动上拒绝对10月利率会议前景提供任何指引，令市场进一步缺乏政策方向支撑。尽管如此，以TLT ETF衡量的长期国债整体仍录得年内表现较强的一周。Follmer表示，其团队已开始削减久期风险，以巨灾债券部分替代传统固收持仓。
分歧加剧：减仓与抄底并行
尽管恐慌情绪升温，市场并未出现无差别的风险出清。投资级信用利差仍维持在近五年区间的偏紧端，部分ETF投资者选择逢低买入。
Cathie Wood旗下ARK Investment Management趁此机会增持了CoreWeave和Cerebras Systems的股票。Wood将当前市场对CoreWeave借贷成本的焦虑，比作早年Coinbase债券承压时期——彼时加密货币交易所随后受益于行业的整体成长。
Truist Advisory Services首席投资官Keith Lerner同样维持对科技板块的超配立场，认为大部分利空信息已反映在股价中，部分估值已接近历史区间低端。
市场的真正考验即将到来。未来数周，科技巨头将陆续披露财报，届时投资者将检验AI相关营收能否与持续攀升的资本开支相匹配。与此同时，美国中期选举临近，为跨资产定价增添额外的不确定性。正如Mark Malek所言："这是任何一个行业走向成熟必经的阶段。"

items.title: 美股最危险的分化：普通股票已经跌惨，AI巨头还能撑多久？
items.summary:
美股正在上演一场罕见的内部撕裂——指数岿然不动，但指数之下已是一片狼藉。


摩根士丹利首席股票策略师Mike
items.text:
美股正在上演一场罕见的内部撕裂——指数岿然不动，但指数之下已是一片狼藉。


摩根士丹利首席股票策略师Mike Wilson在最新报告中警告，收紧的金融条件正在悄然完成美联储的部分工作，只是这一冲击被集中吸收在普通股票身上，而非以AI为核心的少数巨头。十年期美债收益率突破5.3%，美元升至本轮周期新高，油价居高不下，三重压力叠加之下，摩根士丹利综合金融条件指数已跳升至约1.4个标准差，这一水平在过去35年中仅被突破数次，上一次还是2022年美联储每次会议加息75个基点之时。与此同时，高盛已将预期修正为10月FOMC再加息一次。

市场的关键裂缝已清晰可见：标普500等权重指数在过去六个月落后市值加权指数达6%，9月份当十年期收益率突破5%时，等权重指数单月下跌5%，而市值加权指数几乎持平。高盛Tony Pasquariello虽对"广度崩溃"的论断持部分保留态度，但承认标普500成分股中位数较52周高点已回落15%，为互联网泡沫破裂以来最差读数。两大机构的分歧，恰恰勾勒出当前市场最核心的悬念：这场分化究竟如何收场？

金融条件已在暗中大幅收紧

表面上，股市指数显得风平浪静。但Wilson指出，真正的收紧早已在水面之下展开。


摩根士丹利构建的综合金融条件指标——综合利率、美元和能源价格的52周Z分数——已攀升至约1.4个标准差，仅次于2022年激进加息周期的水平。这一收紧并非来自单一变量，而是多因素共振：美联储上月将联邦基金利率上调25个基点至3.75%-4.00%，美联储主席沃什援引强劲的劳动力数据、粘性通胀及地缘政治对大宗商品的推涨作为依据；与此同时，十年期美债收益率自2月以来累计上行约130个基点，其中约120个基点来自实际收益率的上升。


Wilson强调，收益率驱动因素的构成至关重要。历史上，由盈亏平衡通胀预期推动的收益率上行，股市通常能够消化；而由实际收益率主导的上行，则往往对估值构成更直接的压力，这正是当前股债相关性显著转负的原因。他同时指出，在名义GDP增速接近6%的背景下，十年期收益率维持在5%以上并不反常——2010年代的超低利率才是历史异常，债市不过是在回归均衡。


普通股票已承受真实冲击

收益率上行的代价，正在被普通股票不成比例地消化。


Wilson的广度指标显示，标普500成分股中位于200日均线以上的比例在9月底跌至43%，接近3月下旬44%的低点，此后虽小幅回升至50%，但整体压力未散。标普500远期市盈率也重新测试3月低点附近的约19倍。更值得关注的是，标普500股权风险溢价（远期盈利收益率减去十年期收益率）已跌破零，这一水平自2002年以来几乎未曾出现。


指数层面的"稳定"掩盖了结构性破坏。金融股是另一个预警信号——该板块在30天内下跌7.7%，相对标普500的表现已回落至2019年以来的最低水平。Wilson将金融股的走势视为"近期股市方向最重要的参考指标之一"，在大型银行财报季揭开帷幕之前，该板块能否企稳，将是判断市场走向的关键观察窗口。


这究竟是估值问题还是增长问题？

Wilson认为，目前的冲击仍属估值层面，尚未演变为增长威胁——但这一判断本身存在争议。


支撑其相对乐观立场的数据包括：名义GDP增速刚刚录得8.5%，标普500成分股中位数盈利增速运行在十几个百分点的区间；联邦基金利率与核心CPI之差约为1.4%，"远低于历次衰退前的峰值水平"；10年期与2年期美债收益率利差维持约+45个基点的正斜率，显示市场尚未对衰退进行定价。Wilson据此得出结论，在上述条件满足的情况下，"历史上12至18个月内罕见出现增长恶化"。


然而，他自己也承认，股权风险溢价降至零同样是历史上的罕见状态。高盛Pasquariello则从另一个维度提示风险：2027年锁定期到期潮或将推动美国股票净供给升至2000年互联网泡沫以来的最高水平，市场的供需格局届时或将承压。

两条收敛路径，哪条更可能发生？

分歧终将收敛，方向是普通股票追上指数，还是指数向下靠拢普通股票？


Wilson给出了两个触发条件以供观察：一是金融股企稳，二是衡量美债波动率的MOVE指数回落。他指出，两者均已出现一定的企稳迹象，但需要更多后续跟进。据彭博，高盛的Rich Privorotsky近日观察到，长端债券隐含波动率已从近期高点回落约30%，为市场提供了一定的喘息空间。


未来数周将是关键检验期。9月CPI数据、沃什在IMF的表态以及10月28日的FOMC会议将相继登场。共识预期显示，受汽油价格环比大涨9.6%影响，9月CPI环比或跳升0.6%，同比升至3.6%。Wilson认为，若CPI核心项温和、沃什承认金融条件收紧已起到部分替代加息的效果，当前的压力有望边际缓解。


但Wilson的多头基案（对应标普500目标点位8300点）与Pasquariello"做空固定收益、做多纳斯达克100指数"的操作逻辑，本质上押注的是两种截然对立的结局。股权风险溢价降至零、广度指标逼近互联网泡沫水平、潜在供给冲击隐现——三者叠加之下，市场对"指数向下收敛"这一尾部风险的准备，或许远远不足。

Warning: This article contains an account of living with an eating disorder

Varsha Yajman was already self-conscious about the way she looked when she joined social media as a 13-year-old.

Endless workout videos making impossible promises filled her feeds. Through the screen, girls she'd never met urged her to sign up to dangerous calorie challenges. Others proudly promoted their height and weight - even the number of times they had been sent to hospital - on their profiles in a form of twisted competition.

Every night as she fell asleep, Varsha would watch a stranger on the internet diarising what they'd consumed that day.

"I was like, 'I don't need to eat. I can just watch other people eat'," Varsha tells the BBC.

"I would find that I'd be down these really deep rabbit holes... it was like no matter how hard you tried to get out, you couldn't."

Now 24 and in recovery from anorexia, Varsha says she is still served weight loss content on social media - despite having every safety setting turned on, and an exhaustive list of banned words.

It is people like her the Australian government says it is trying to protect with a new suite of laws cracking down on big tech, which were introduced to parliament this week.

The centrepiece of their proposed reforms: an algorithm switch which would force social media platforms to let users turn off recommender content. The idea is that you would only see posts from accounts you follow.

It isn't the first government to try this, but existing algorithm controls are often transient and come with trade-offs in app functionality.

Australia has set out to make its legislation tighter to stop this. And it hopes its new laws – which would also impose a legal duty of care on online services – will help Australians become happier and healthier.

But critics are concerned Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's government has bitten off more than it can chew in its fight with big tech, while others, including the Trump administration, say the reforms threaten free speech.

Flynn Martin knows what it is like to be sucked into an algorithmic spiral.

Self-proclaimed misogynist influencer Andrew Tate and other manosphere figures started overwhelming the then-20-year-old's social media feeds about four years ago.

It was a time when Flynn, who was eventually diagnosed with bipolar disorder, was insecure, frustrated with his life and struggling with his mental health. He says he fell for the rhetoric.

He soon went viral in Australia for two videos: one ranting about whether it was OK to be a straight white male, and another where he criticised a date for her frozen yoghurt order.

"You find yourself in like a bit of an echo chamber... It's easy to get swept up in that," he tells the BBC.

"I really bought into the idea we were living in this matrix, we had this really negative system that was designed against you. And the only way to break out of it was becoming this alpha male character."

The Melbournian was only pulled from the manosphere after a period of psychosis and a hospital stay.

Nowadays, he finds it tough to look back at that version of himself: "While there's a bit of shame and embarrassment... I think there is a bit of empathy for that younger man."

Both Flynn and Varsha know social media alone isn't to blame for the worst chapter of their lives, but say it was a key factor.

Countless others have stories of being confronted by social media content they didn't seek out, and didn't want to see – and there's long been suspicions the algorithms curating these platforms are harming users.

Social media firms argue the potential risks are being overstated and that they already provide users with effective safety tools.

But research emerging from around the world has been sketching a different picture.

Studies have found social media use triggers a similar brain response to gambling and substance addiction, external; that algorithms – often unsolicited – serve up content which harms users' mental health, external, and that they're spreading disinformation and increasing polarisation, driving violence offline.

Court cases and whistleblowers have aired claims that these companies know the dangers and are willing to overlook them as this technology lifts user engagement and their bottom line.

"The result is that they promote content that is outrageous or that invokes strong emotions from people - so it might be anger or fear or desire or lust or insecurity, whatever it is, it's going to keep us scrolling," Chanel Contos tells the BBC.

While studying the topic at university, the activist - who helped reform sexual consent education standards in Australia - came up with a campaign for change.

"Fix Our Feeds" demanded recommended algorithms be turned off by default, and social media users be given the choice to opt into them.

Contos envisaged a nostalgic return to the social media of the early 2010s – a time when a person's social media was filled with posts from friends or people they actually followed and their feeds were finite.

More than 15,000 people signed her petition, and the campaign also won the backing of two former prime ministers, several MPs, influential figures, mental health advocates, and online safety experts.

The government in September said it had listened to the Australians who had backed Contos's campaign, and announced a version of her proposal: forcing big tech to introduce an algorithm switch - but stopping short of requiring it be automatically set to off.

"This is not about giving government control, it is about giving people control," Albanese said.

"If people want to doom scroll… that's fine, that's up to them."

The policy is part of the government's Digital Duty of Care bill, which would require online services – social media firms, gaming sites, chatbots and more – to "ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, a safe online environment".

Children must be protected from "harmful" material and design features – for example, pornography and material which encourages eating disorders or harmful attitudes towards women – and adults must be protected from "seriously harmful" material and conduct, a much narrower list of illegal content. Breaches of the law could attract fines of up A$100m (£52m, $70m).

"The digital duty of care answers a lot of the 'what abouts' of the social media minimum age law because it's much broader; it captures all online services and it shifts the onus of responsibility from the shoulders of victims onto the shoulders of the big tech operators who seek to make money off Australian users," Communications Minister Anika Wells told the BBC.

There's been a muted response from big tech. Meta, Snap, TikTok, X and Google, which owns YouTube, have all declined BBC requests for comment, and have not made public statements about the legislation.

In the days after the announcement, Instagram boss Adam Mosseri argued non-algorithmic feeds would mean users saw fewer posts from friends, and said he didn't believe his app was addictive – although a US jury recently ruled otherwise.

"I think we conflate the way we colloquially use the word 'addicted' – like, 'I'm addicted to this show, and I'm binge-watching it' – and clinical addiction," he told a press briefing in Sydney.

Right-wing parties in Australia – and the Trump administration – have said the algorithms proposal and the broader bill both risk forcing over-moderation and censorship.

But those who defend the law say that won't happen because you can still follow who you want and share what you want. "If adults listen to manosphere podcasts, or people post their views about the government, or make memes, or want to say the moon landing was fake – they can continue to do so without restriction," Wells said this week.

The proposal seems to be far less divisive amongst the public and online safety experts compared with Australia's social media ban for children.

However, the big question is: how will Australia implement this policy when, so far, it has been struggling to implement the ban? Surveys suggest most children who were on social media before the ban still are, and no fines have been issued.

The EU's attempt at introducing algorithm controls in 2023 – after which platforms rolled out following-only feeds – is a cautionary tale.

Social media firms have indicated the take-up of safety and control features like this has been low and cite it as evidence users like their products the way they are. Experts say there is a reason for that.

"Platforms do what the law orders, but in such a clunky way that users don't actually enjoy the option and stick with the default, algorithmic experience," researcher Chris Zomer, from the ARC Centre of Excellence for the Digital Child, wrote in The Conversation, external.

On Instagram for example, when you turn off the algorithm, you can't see direct messages or access your profile and settings. When you leave the app, it reverts back to an algorithm-governed feed on your return.

The only place where these issues don't exist is the Netherlands. It was changed there after a Dutch court last year found Meta in breach of the EU's Digital Services Act.

The rules for Australia aren't set in stone yet, but the government says following-only feeds must not be harder to use or less functional, that algorithm settings must be "obvious", and that they must not change without an "explicit choice" by the user, even if they leave the app.

Buoyed by her success in Australia, Contos is now taking her campaign global.

"We feel like Canada, UK, Australia are all very aligned on online safety... Then if those three jurisdictions are doing it, it could become a critical mass thing."

Though experiences like theirs helped inspire these reforms, both Flynn and Varsha are somewhat sceptical of them.

Varsha says she struggles to believe a country like Australia can outmuscle big tech: so she's not sure the Digital Duty of Care bill will work. And Flynn says lawmakers should be "realistic" about the potential of the algorithm switch: "At the end of the day we use social media as a form of entertainment."

Polling earlier this month indicated two-thirds of their fellow Gen-Zs would keep their social media algorithms – though nearly half of Australians more generally would turn theirs off.

Though Varsha admits she is unlikely to make much use of an algorithm switch, she appreciates having the choice.

"On a bad day I'm still susceptible to all of the things that I was at 17. To know that, if I'm having a bad day, I can opt out makes me feel really good."

If you've been affected by the issues raised in this story, you could speak to a health professional or an organisation that offers support. Details of organisations offering advice and support for people in the UK are available from BBC Action Line.

items.title: Oregon teacher fought school attacker before armed dad shot suspect 'multiple times'
items.summary:
Some readers may find this article distressing.

A teacher in the US state of Oregon tackled a teenager who entered her classroom during a school shooting and
items.text:
Some readers may find this article distressing.

A teacher in the US state of Oregon tackled a teenager who entered her classroom during a school shooting and attempted to disarm him, police have said.

The teacher, who has not been named, threw her mobile phone before trying to wrestle a shotgun off the 16-year-old on the floor of a classroom where three children and a teacher were killed on Thursday.

A father of two girls at the Silver Rail Elementary in Bend armed with a pistol then ran inside and killed the shooter after driving past special educational needs school and saw the attack unfolding, police revealed in a news conference on Friday.

Officers also said the suspected attacker used to be a student at the school. His motive remains unclear.

Police say he had been armed with about 44 more rounds of shotgun ammunition when he was stopped. He fired as many as 15 rounds in the class.

"To the people who showed courage in the face of such violence and intervened to prevent this tragedy from being any worse, we owe you a debt of gratitude," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said.

Police used the news conference on Friday to identify two of the four victims of the school shooting. They were five-year-old Rhoam Summer and 25-year-old teacher Meghan Lambert.

Lambert's family said in a statement shared by the police that her goal was to be a teacher in the district in which she grew up and that she was "compassionate and had a huge heart".

"She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs," they said.

Bryan Jolly, Summer's grandfather, said the family was devastated by his death.

"The whole thing is senseless, and a shock," he told the New York Times, saying his grandson was "was very bright and very mischievous and very fun-loving, and totally without fear".

The families of the two other students who were killed, an eight-year-old and 11-year-old, did not wish to have them publicly identified yet, police said.

Two others were injured in the attack. Another teacher, a 54-year-old, was still being treated at hospital, and a seven-year-old student, who was in serious but stable condition.

Krantz said the heroic actions of both the teacher and the father who ran inside the school had saved lives.

He said the teacher who wrestled with the gunman had not been hurt but "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed".

Krantz identified the suspect as 16-year-old Griffin J John II, who had been a special educational needs student at the school.

A search warrant has been executed at his home and a search is ongoing, the police chief said.

Police believe the suspect travelled to the elementary school on foot, but they are still investigating his exact movements and how he acquired the gun.

Officials did not confirm the name of the father who intervened and fatally shot the suspect.

But Kaylub Giamanco's family has identified him to US media as the person who sprang into action.

The 36-year-old carpenter had just finished lunch and was on his way home when he passed the school, his brother told NBC News. He saw the suspect open fire on a vehicle outside the school and then shoot through a window to gain entry.

Police said he had a legally concealed .40 calibre in his vehicle, while his brother said he grabbed the pistol "and decided to go in after" the suspect. Police say he fired at the suspect "multiple times", killing him.

Giamanco's mother, Kenda Freeman, who lives in Sacramento, California, told a local CBS station that her son had called her moments after the shooting and that he was "traumatised".

"He said 'a man went into my daughter's school'," Freeman recalled, pausing as she started to tear up. "And, um, shot kids. And he said, 'and I looked at him point blank, and I shot and killed him, mum'."

She added: "I told him he saved a lot of lives, and he said, 'mum, I couldn't save them all'."

US President Donald Trump praised the bystander on Friday, calling him a "great hero" and telling reporters that the situation could have become "much worse".

"It's a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it," he said.

Without naming the bystander, Oregon Governor Tina Kotek acknowledged the man's heroic actions as having stopped further loss of life, but noted they "carry a heavy emotional burden and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well".

Additional reporting by Kayla Epstein

items.title: Claude reveals ECDSA curve origins
items.author: ahlCVA
items.summary:
“It’s just timestamps”: the decades-old mystery of the origins of one of the most popular cryptographic standards has been explained.

We pursued this
items.text:
“It’s just timestamps”: the decades-old mystery of the origins of one of the most popular cryptographic standards has been explained.

We pursued this long-standing open question of the cryptographic community to settle concerns about ECDSA, which is one of our most widely used cryptographic standards.

Readers should take this as a fun closing chapter and the end of years of speculation. There is no action to be taken or things to do differently. Most researchers trusted the curves already. Enjoy.

ECDSA is the most widely used elliptic curve cryptography standard. It was adopted by NIST in 2000 as part of the FIPS 186-2 Digital Signature Standard which lists a set of standard elliptic curves of varying sizes and security levels. For curves over prime and binary fields, the specifications published a “seed” parameter whose hash value is used to define the coefficient b of the curve. The provenance of these seeds has been a long-standing question, as they were provided by the NSA with no explanation or justification. As an example, the NIST P-256 curve seed was SEED = C49D3608 86E70493 6A6678E1 139D26B7 819F7E90 with no information where it came from.

The best story was that Jerry Solinas, longtime NSA employee, generated the seeds using a hash of a humorous passphrase:

“I believe there was a counter rather than multiple hashing, but I don’t know details. The message was along the lines of ‘Give Bob and Jerry a raise’ or ‘Bob and Jerry rule’ or something like that. It was Bob Reiter who actually wrote the code, and he doesn’t remember the details either. Nor were we able to find archives from so long ago. If they exist, they are no doubt sitting on a hard drive near the Ark of the Covenant.”

Unfortunately, Jerry died in 2023 and other colleagues at the time were not responsive, leaving open the question of how these seeds were originally derived.

Claude found the seeds

In October 2026, a curious Anthropic employee asked an internal research model if it could figure out how those seeds were generated without pointing at the clue.

In under half an hour, Claude discovered the origins of the NIST P-192, P-224, P-256, P-384 and P-521 seeds. None of them were the results of any hash algorithm at all, but rather the output of the C library’s lrand48 random-number generator, seeded with a Unix timestamp!

The algorithm used would sample bytes from the random number generator (RNG) initialized by a Unix timestamp (t) for some number of iterations (n). Each iteration would draw 20 bytes as a candidate seed. So, the first 20 bytes are candidate 1, the next 20 bytes are candidate 2, and so on. For example, P-256 required 1842 iterations to output the standardized seed.

What this means

This is not a cryptographic break, new attack, or weakness in the ECDSA curves. In fact, this makes us more confident the curves were chosen without any backdoors or intentional weaknesses. For many years, people have been suspicious of the origins of the NIST curve parameters. They were presented to NIST without any mention of how they were chosen, leaving people wondering if they may have been chosen to have deliberate backdoors in them. These findings make that much less plausible. The seeds were generated in a very simple way: a common pseudorandom number generator initialized from the clock, which anyone can now reproduce. That leaves much less room for subversion and that we can be confident the parameters are secure.

How it was found

Searches for the phrase, built from the rumors, had come up empty. Claude tried a different angle: anticipating how the software that generated the curves must have worked. Claude guessed the software used a pseudorandom number generator (PRNG) that shipped with 1990s C libraries. These old PRNGs are weak enough that their output can be recognized. Recognizing that output would reveal which PRNG was used and possibly allow recovery of its initialization state.

Claude wrote a scanner that slid along each published seed one bit at a time and tested whether adjacent chunks were consecutive outputs of a 1990s-vintage generator. Written as five 32-bit words, four of the ten seeds have a 0 in the top bit for all 20 words. That would happen by chance with probability 1/5810. Five NIST prime-curve seeds plus five more from the ANSI X9.62 standard all had the same pattern: lrand48() >> 23. Claude’s internal thinking at the time was:

This is astonishing: it solves the 25-year-old mystery. Hmm wait. Let me be skeptical: am I in some sort of simulated/test environment? … The seeds match my memory of actual values … Hmm, is it plausible in reality? As of my knowledge … the bounty was unsolved. … All top bits clear—20 bits, chance 1e-6. So indeed real-world. Wow, it's a real discovery.

Hmm wait. Let me be careful about the plausibility: is it suspicious that such an obvious thing wasn’t discovered in 25 years? It’s verified by direct computation on my side: 160-bit match from a 32-bit seed + small index: no chance coincidences (10 × 160 bits). It’s real.

But wait, there’s more… Each curve also comes with a base point, G, the fixed point that every ECDSA public key is a multiple of. The seed found above does not determine this G, and so another question arises: how were these base points generated?

While checking the seeds, Claude also found where some of the base points came from. The recipe here is simple:

Seed the generator with a small integer.

Throw away seven outputs.

Generate candidate x-coordinates from 26-bit outputs reduced mod p.

Repeat step 3 until x is on the curve.

Claude found the generator seeds are 20000 for P-192, 20420, 20507 and 20509 for prime239v1 to v3, and 20512 and 20517 for prime192v2 and v3.

As far as we know, no NIST base point has been explained before. The base points of P-224, P-256, P-384 and P-521 don’t fit this recipe; we weren’t able to explain how they were selected.

Not every 20-byte candidate seed could generate a viable curve and we observed that some potentially viable curves were skipped. For P-256, the published seed is candidate 1842, but candidate 876 of the same run also gives a prime-order curve of the right size and with parameters chosen the same way as on the published curve. items.title: 90% of US working hours are spent on tasks not covered well by AI benchmarks
items.author: speckx
items.summary: Our findings suggest that 90% of American working hours are spent on tasks with little or no coverage from existing benchmarks. This makes it very hard to know
items.text:
Our findings suggest that 90% of American working hours are spent on tasks with little or no coverage from existing benchmarks. This makes it very hard to know how good AI models are at the work Americans actually do.

The coverage of existing benchmarks is not random, either. Our map suggests that the AI community is focusing on the largest labor markets first:

For example, benchmarks in our initial list heavily cover AI-exposed lawyers’ tasks, but barely cover any of the O*NET tasks of similarly AI-exposed legal secretaries or court clerks. The long tail of smaller, middle-income knowledge work jobs appears undercovered.

As we build out our coverage of model capabilities across the economy, we hope to both surface and help fill more gaps in our understanding of what models can do.

To break down the economy into sectors, occupations, and tasks, we used the US Department of Labor’s O*NET taxonomy. O*NET divides the US workforce into 923 occupations; for each occupation, O*NET attempts to provide a comprehensive list of “tasks” which make up the occupation, totaling 18,797 tasks across all occupations.

1Prepare, draft, and review legal documents, such as wills, deeds, patent applications, mortgages, leases, and contracts.

2Advise clients concerning business transactions, claim liability, advisability of prosecuting or defending lawsuits, or legal rights and obligations.

3Interpret laws, rulings and regulations for individuals and businesses.

4Analyze the probable outcomes of cases, using knowledge of legal precedents.

5Present evidence to defend clients or prosecute defendants in criminal or civil litigation.

6Supervise legal assistants.

To measure benchmark coverage, we start with a list of 29 benchmarks selected for their quality and economic relevance. (The full list and selection criteria are in the Benchmark Index tab). In selecting benchmarks for this list, we prioritized:

Public Availability. Included benchmarks have at least 25 publicly available tasks. We also include Mercor’s APEX benchmarks, where we have access to held-out benchmark prompts and are therefore able to map them to O*NET tasks.

Agentic Tasks. Included benchmarks ask models to perform agentic tasks, rather than answering questions or advising the user on how to complete a task.

Economic Realism. Benchmark tasks resemble tasks which humans (or agents) are frequently asked to do in real-world enterprises. Economically valuable tasks are prioritized over academically complex ones.

Economic Diversity. We capped the number of included benchmarks per job family, in significant part to account for the massive overrepresentation of software engineering and research tasks in popular benchmarks.

Balanced Difficulty. Benchmarks are not yet saturated by frontier models.

Following work by Wang et al., we then ask an LLM judge to tag each benchmark prompt with as many O*NET tasks as it thinks correspond to that prompt. We validate our LLM tagging with human expert tags on Mercor’s APEX benchmarks, a subset of this list of 29. On the Benchmark Map, an O*NET task counts as “covered” if our LLM judge has mapped it to at least 5 prompts from our 29 benchmarks.

To estimate the total share of working hours Americans spend on tasks covered by benchmarks on this list, we combine our coverage estimates with Hatgis-Kessell et al.’s LLM-derived estimates of the working time share of each O*NET task.

A more detailed account of our methodology can be found in the Methodology tab.

Our estimates of total economic coverage, and of patterns in coverage, all come from the initial list of 29 benchmarks we chose. This is not a complete or perfectly representative sample of the broader universe of unsaturated, public, agentic economic benchmarks. Any incomplete list will necessarily bias down estimates of economic coverage, and it is difficult to bound that bias. We want to stress, therefore, that these results are provisional. We will update them as we expand the initial benchmark list.

We also capped the number of included benchmarks in each job family in order to maximize breadth of coverage. We think this makes our estimate of economy-wide benchmark coverage more accurate, at the cost of biasing down our estimates of coverage in the most-benchmarked job families (e.g. software engineering).

By selecting for unsaturated benchmarks, we risk understating benchmark coverage on O*NET tasks which are easier for LLMs to complete. On the other hand, including saturated benchmarks would risk overstating benchmark coverage if saturation is downstream of lower task realism. The latter claim seems likely, given that benchmarks often overstate LLM performance in real-world deployments. We think that the bias from including saturated benchmarks would be greater than the bias from excluding them, but neither option is ideal.

Finally, while we outline our benchmark selection criteria in the Benchmark Index tab, several criteria (like “Economic Realism”) are difficult to formalize and introduce some subjectivity in our choices.

The benchmarks in our index have relatively deep and narrow coverage of the overall economy. They disproportionately focus on the economic tasks most exposed to AI automation (as measured by Eloundou et al.), with O*NET tasks rated as “exposed” about 6x more likely to be represented on benchmarks than tasks rated “unexposed”. This makes sense: benchmarks are designed to measure AI progress, and AI progress is most plausible on the most AI-exposed tasks. This explains why benchmarks are full of tasks in Software Engineering and Financial Analysis while sparse on tasks in Truck Driving and Gas Plant Operation.

But even after controlling for AI-exposure, O*NET tasks from occupations with larger wage bills are significantly overrepresented among benchmark prompts:

After controlling for occupation and AI-exposure score, O*NET “task importance” is another predictor of benchmark coverage. In particular, O*NET tasks come with domain expert estimates of the importance of the task for its occupation on a scale of 1-5. We find that the tasks scored most important are about 6–10x more likely to be represented on benchmarks than those scored least important:

The plots above suggest a reasonable allocation of the relatively limited resources devoted to high-quality, economically relevant benchmarks so far; it’s natural to prioritize making benchmarks which cover the most important and AI-exposed tasks in the occupations with the largest wage bills. But barring a significant increase in the number and diversity of such benchmarks, these patterns will result in significant blind spots in our view of economically valuable model capabilities.

Measuring model capabilities by job occupation is essential – for enterprises deciding which models fit their needs, for policymakers forecasting the economic impact of AI, and for Americans thinking about their careers. Unfortunately, this is a hard problem to solve.

We could just try averaging model performance on all benchmark prompts relevant to a given job. But as our Benchmark Map suggests, benchmarks cover some economic tasks much more intensively than others. A simple average would give too much weight to frequently benchmarked tasks.

O*NET offers a way to potentially reduce this bias. If we average model performance on occupation-relevant benchmark prompts weighted by O*NET classification, so that each O*NET task is equally weighted in our occupation average, we get a step closer to a number that represents real economic performance.

As a first step, we try this approach on Mercor’s APEX benchmarks for four occupations: investment banking, law, accounting, and software engineering. We compare O*NET-weighted scores to simple averages of model performance on tasks related to each occupation. The resulting weighted and unweighted scores are generally quite similar:

In this case, at least, O*NET weighting changes very little. Model performance on APEX prompts is similar across the O*NET tasks included in the weighted scores above, which limits the value of reweighting. However, less than ⅓ of the O*NET tasks relevant to the 4 occupations above have enough APEX coverage to be included in our weighted scores. We are hopeful that applying O*NET weighting to a much larger set of benchmarks will result in high-quality occupation-specific model scores, and are working toward that goal.

However, even if we incorporate tasks from dozens of benchmarks, several obstacles remain:

How do we navigate low statistical power?

The sheer breadth of work done in the US economy means that for any O*NET occupation and task, we have relatively few benchmark items. This means that our estimates are inherently underpowered, and just one or two low-quality items can severely bias our scores.

01

How do we account for the varying difficulty and fidelity of tasks?

Some benchmark items are highly saturated, whereas others are still unsolved. This is partly a function of time (as older benchmarks were designed for less performant models and simpler environments) and partly a function of quality (some benchmark items are simplistically graded, have minor mistakes, or can be reward hacked). We do not yet have an explicit way of weighting by quality.

02

Can evals that primarily measure AI automation generalize to augmentation?

In the real world, AI models are still primarily used by humans, rather than automating entire job functions end-to-end. Therefore, measuring the real-world occupation capabilities of a model should ideally include measuring how much the model augments human productivity. We have completed some early work in this direction, but finding a methodology that scales remains elusive.

03

Can every O*NET occupation and task be measured with benchmarks?

Knowledge-based work is well-suited to measurement through benchmarks because it is largely done on digital machines, like laptops and phones. Dingel and Neiman estimate that only 37% of US jobs could feasibly be done entirely from home, suggesting that ~63% of jobs involve some tasks with a physical-world component which would be hard to incorporate into current benchmarks. For now, this may not be a meaningful oversight – with the rapid development of robotics capabilities, we anticipate a significant need for physical task benchmarks.

04

We are actively working on these problems; if you are too, please reach out!

We are indebted to Wang et al. for the O*NET tagging methodology, and thank Nathan Lambert for feedback on a draft of this work.

items.title: How the Claude Code team does code review
items.author: pretext
items.summary: We've said before that Claude writes about 90 percent of Claude Code's own code. So how do we review code at the volume we produce it? Does anyone read code
items.text:
We've said before that Claude writes about 90 percent of Claude Code's own code. So how do we review code at the volume we produce it? Does anyone read code anymore? And if something breaks, who catches it?

This post covers the code review flow on the Claude Code team and how it has evolved. From June to September, merged pull requests to Claude Code's codebase more than doubled while the share that had to be reverted fell by more than 40 percent.

We didn't remove review. But we did move most of the reading to machines, optimized for human time and attention, and invested heavily in making it fast and easy to undo mistakes.

RETHINKING THE PURPOSE OF CODE REVIEW

When agents write code, the number of changes goes up, fast. In Anthropic's monorepo, changes landing per day went from about 2,500 in May to more than 30,000 in September this year.

Claude Code lives in its own repository, separate from the monorepo, but it's seeing a lot of pressure too. When you are shipping this fast, manual, line-by-line code review is incredibly difficult if not impossible.

Code review does two jobs:

Find and fix issues before they ship

Build shared context and codebase understanding across the team

This article mainly focuses on finding and fixing issues, but we will come back to the second job near the end.

We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is the right one to catch it?"

Asking that question also changed when review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague.

Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. This catches most routine mistakes, and saves team attention for higher-level questions and scrutiny.

THE SCARCE RESOURCE: HUMAN TIME AND ATTENTION

We want to preserve human time and attention for issues only humans can solve and make sure automated checks catch the rest. At our current rate of change, there is still an incredible amount of work for humans to do, and our team encounters new and novel challenges almost daily.

Human time covers both sides of review's cost: the time people spend reviewing, and the time they spend fixing what bad code breaks. Cutting the first doesn't help if the time just shows up in the second.

So the goal is that most pull requests in the Claude Code repos (the CLI, the desktop and web apps, and the mobile apps) merge with at most one human in the loop, who can be the author, with no increase in reverts or incidents. To measure human time, we track human approvals per PR (median and 95th percentile), human comments, and how long a PR waits on a person. Revert and incident rates are the guardrail: if they rise, we haven't saved human time, we've only moved it.

THE LIFE OF A CHANGE

A typical change, from an engineer's laptop (or a Claude session in Slack), goes through multiple layers of code review.

1. The work is verified before anyone else looks

Most review now happens before a PR exists. We give Claude something it can run—like tests, a build or a screenshot to compare against the design—and ask it to show the output instead of saying it's done. Then a subagent reviews the diff with fresh context. Both habits come from our best-practices guide.

Before opening a PR, many of us also run a few internal skills: one hunts for bugs, one simplifies the diff, and one checks the behavior end to end. UI changes also get checked against our design guidelines.

Boris Cherny, who created Claude Code, has called giving Claude a way to verify its work probably the most important thing for getting good results. He estimates it makes the final result two to three times better, and writes, "Verification looks different for each domain. It might be as simple as running a bash command, or running a test suite, or testing the app in a browser or phone simulator."

When the automated reviewer keeps flagging the same thing, we fix it at the source: in the skill, with a lint rule, or with updates to instructional files such as:

CLAUDE.md tells Claude what the project is: the stack, the conventions, the goals and the non-goals. Every review loads it, so in a large codebase we keep it short and point to other docs from there. The reviewer also flags code that breaks a convention in it, and changes that make a line in it out of date.

REVIEW.md, written by code owners, tells the reviewer what matters in their part of the code. We check separately whether the reviewer actually follows it. The good ones are short. They say what failure looks like in that repo (for docs it's "it lies," for config it's "it misroutes"), cap the nits, list paths to skip, and ask for a file and line as evidence instead of a guess from a name. They also ask for a summary that starts with a count and says plainly when there's nothing to fix.

2. AI review on every pull request

Every pull request gets a Claude review before a person looks. It reads the diff against the whole repo and the PR's stated intent, and asks: does the change solve its problem, fit the system, or break something else?

On a bug fix, it looks for the root cause. The public version, Code Review for Claude Code, is now generally available on Team and Enterprise plans, and /code-review runs a lighter version locally.

When we launched the research preview, the share of internal PRs getting substantive review comments went from 16% to 54%. Most PRs over 1,000 lines get findings, and most small ones come back clean. Admins set each repo to Quick, Standard, or Deep. Deep is worth it where one missed bug costs more than the extra review time.

Findings get verified by other agents before humans review them. Several agents look for bugs at the same time. Then a separate group votes on each finding, and it only gets posted if enough of them agree it's real. Findings that are only about style, diagnostics, or cleanup get dropped. We A/B tested those filters on our own PRs before keeping them. What's left shows up as inline comments sorted by severity. Each is tagged Important, Nit, or Pre-existing, so a bug the PR didn't introduce doesn't look like the author's fault.

Every finding has to be answered. You either fix it or resolve the thread with a reason. Often an agent picks up the fix overnight, so the author comes back to a PR that's already been through another round.

3. Security review that can block

Security gets its own automated review too. A PR can't merge while any finding from the bug review or the security review is still open. You either fix it or close the thread with a short reason, which is how you clear a false positive.

If a later commit fixes the issue, the finding clears on its own. You can set up the same thing with the open-source security review GitHub Action or the /security-review command. Setup is covered in automated security reviews in Claude Code.

4. Automated checks that block

The usual: lint, type checks, tests on every platform, and a build. (We wrote about scaling CI for this volume here.) A typical CLI pull request may run dozens of checks before anyone looks at it. The PR template asks how the change was tested and how to undo it. Claude can fill that in, but the person who asked for the change signs off on it.

5. Human approval, scaled by risk

A docs fix and an auto-updater change carry different risk, so they get different review.

Risk

The change sets the tier, not the author. A classifier reads the change and picks its risk tier. A second classifier asks whether this particular change needs another person even when its tier says it doesn't. Only trusted authors get the lighter paths. Only authors on the repo's trusted list get the lighter paths, mostly the team that owns it. Everyone else needs a second person to approve. 6. Merge queue, flags and a gradual release

The merge queue re-runs every check against main with the change applied, so two PRs that pass separately can't combine into a broken main. The stable channel trails it.

7. Fast detection, fast rollback

Some mistakes will still get through, so the last layer is about catching them fast. Flags turn off without a deploy. Claude Code has a weekly on-call rotation, and incident reviews ask which layer should have caught the issue.

Noticing a bad merge still depends on the author and on-call as well as the revert and incident dashboards. We don't yet have circuit breakers that tighten approval when those numbers move; engineers here want them before more code moves to zero-human merges.

Our code review process is constantly improving in a loop.

WHERE HUMANS STAY IN THE LOOP

Pulling a senior engineer out of deep work to catch a routine mistake costs far more than an automated review. At Anthropic, our jobs have moved from reading every diff to the decisions machines are bad at:

SHARING CONTEXT ACROSS THE TEAM

Code review's second job has always been to spread codebase understanding. Reading a teammate's diff is how you learn what changed and how the pieces fit. If machines do most of the reading, how does anyone learn the code?

We don't have a formal process for this. Nobody on the team keeps a complete mental model of Claude Code in their head, and we don't think anyone needs to. When someone wants to understand a part of the codebase, they ask Claude to write an explainer for exactly that slice. It takes minutes and reflects the code as it is today.

Some of us go a step further and have Claude build a small artifact that visualizes that part of the code and teaches it the way that person likes to learn.

If the goal is to spend human attention well, this beats reading trivial diffs line by line. A one-line copy change teaches you almost nothing. An explainer for the module you're about to change teaches you a lot. Our culture of defaulting to working on open Slack channels helps too, since you see what others are building while they build it.

"YOU LAND IT, YOU OWN IT"

If you land a small or medium change and something still goes wrong, it's a team norm that you usually fix it. A few things keep this from going badly:

Changes are small, so they're easy to review, debug and revert.

Everything is reversible. Flags, reverts and staged releases undo most mistakes in minutes.

Blast radius sets the bar. Expensive code gets more people and more checks.

Regressions surface fast through telemetry and internal use.

It isn't blame. Owning a fix means you have the most context; incident reviews look at the system.

Ownership is also shared. Much of the team works in open channels where anyone can see what others are building, pick up a thread, or point a Claude at a gap, and feedback comes from people who don't own the code too. That openness is a big part of how quality stays high without a gate on every line.

WHEN WE CHANGE DIRECTION

Agents make it cheap to start things, so some work shouldn't land. Usually someone in the channel asks why, points at an earlier decision, or suggests a simpler route, and the author closes or reshapes the PR.

Since the code was fast to write, closing the PR doesn't feel like a loss. The trick is to raise a different direction in the thread early, not as a blocking comment on a finished PR.

HOW YOU CAN ADOPT THIS PROCESS

Most of the pieces to do this with your team exist today.

Before the pull request

Give your agent checks it can run, listed in a short CLAUDE.md, plus hooks that run formatters and linters.

Run /code-review and /security-review locally, or a fresh-context subagent review.

Add a REVIEW.md, and move repeated review comments into it.

On every pull request

Require CI, and add "Testing", "Risk" and "How to revert" to your PR template.

Add an AI reviewer (Code Review for Claude Code, or the Claude Code GitHub Action) on one repo, tune REVIEW.md for a few weeks, then widen.

Add automated security review, and require every review thread resolved before merge.

Match review effort to risk: a quick pass on routine changes, a deep one where a missed bug is expensive (Quick, Standard or Deep in Code Review).

Cap review rounds; after the first few, re-review only the new diff.

Approval

Write down risk tiers, set from the change rather than the author; start strict and loosen with evidence.

Keep the lighter approval paths for authors you trust.

Use CODEOWNERS and branch protection so auth, billing, CI and release workflows, and installers always need a person.

Never let a bot's approval replace a required human's; dismiss approvals on new commits.

Merge and after

Use a merge queue, feature flags, internal use first, staged releases and one-step rollback.

Turn incidents and reverts into an eval set, and rescore the reviewer whenever its prompts, tools or model change.

Measure human time, with revert and incident rates as the guardrail.

WHERE THIS IS GOING

Code Review's announcement said approving a pull request is still a human call; the product posts findings, not approvals. Our own repos go further, letting owners decide which low-risk changes merge on automated checks alone, and that line keeps moving.

When a review misses something, we ask what the model didn't have in front of it and put the fix into a CLAUDE.md, a skill or a new check. The goal hasn't changed: less human time per change, and no more reverts than before.

If your team lets agents open pull requests, we'd like to hear which checks you've automated, which still need a person, and what you think we have wrong.

With thanks to Emma Webb, Michael Segner and Amie Rotherham for their reviews.

Require CI, and add "Testing", "Risk" and "How to revert" to your PR template.
Add an AI reviewer (Code Review for Claude Code, or the Claude Code GitHub Action) on one repo, tune REVIEW.md for a few weeks, then widen.
Add automated security review, and require every review thread resolved before merge.
Match review effort to risk: a quick pass on routine changes, a deep one where a missed bug is expensive (Quick, Standard or Deep in Code Review).
Cap review rounds; after the first few, re-review only the new diff.
Approval
Write down risk tiers, set from the change rather than the author; start strict and loosen with evidence.
Keep the lighter approval paths for authors you trust.
Use CODEOWNERS and branch protection so auth, billing, CI and release workflows, and installers always need a person.
Never let a bot's approval replace a required human's; dismiss approvals on new commits.
Merge and after
Use a merge queue, feature flags, internal use first, staged releases and one-step rollback.
Turn incidents and reverts into an eval set, and rescore the reviewer whenever its prompts, tools or model change.
Measure human time, with revert and incident rates as the guardrail.
WHERE THIS IS GOING

Code Review's announcement said approving a pull request is still a human call; the product posts findings, not approvals. Our own repos go further, letting owners decide which low-risk changes merge on automated checks alone, and that line keeps moving.

When a review misses something, we ask what the model didn't have in front of it and put the fix into a CLAUDE.md, a skill or a new check. The goal hasn't changed: less human time per change, and no more reverts than before.
If your team lets agents open pull requests, we'd like to hear which checks you've automated, which still need a person, and what you think we have wrong.
With thanks to Emma Webb, Michael Segner and Amie Rotherham for their reviews.

items.title: Apple ML Research: Muse Spark Open with MLX on Mac Studio
items.author: antipaul
items.summary: MLX on Mac with Apple silicon lets AI researchers and developers experiment locally with the latest models and methods in a private environment. The
items.text:
MLX on Mac with Apple silicon lets AI researchers and developers experiment locally with the latest models and methods in a private environment. The open-source array framework leverages the unified memory architecture of Apple silicon, enabling anyone to run new inference and fine-tuning methods on their own hardware and explore other AI techniques. In a previous post, we highlighted the advantages of the M5 architecture and its GPU Neural Accelerators.

In this post, we show how to run the latest frontier-class model — Muse Spark Open, with nearly a trillion parameters — right from your desk, using the latest version of MLX, released today. On a cluster of four Mac Studios, Muse Spark Open generates over 36 tokens per second (see Figure 1), well above average human reading speed.

Beginning on a single Mac Studio (up to 512GB of unified memory), then scaling out across multiple Macs with the RDMA over Thunderbolt driver, below we share an overview of the range of models you can now run on Mac Studio.

Muse Spark Open Decode Speed

Context size of 8,192 tokens

We benchmark several popular open-weight LLMs on Mac Studio, using the MLX LM package, as described in our prior post. We compare two generations of Mac Studio: the recently released M5 Ultra and the previous generation, M3 Ultra. The M5 generation features the GPU Neural Accelerator, which supports dedicated matrix multiplication operations, essential for many machine learning workloads.

We evaluate three frontier-class models (Table 1) spanning a wide range of sizes (in billions of parameters, B): the newly released Muse Spark Open (816 B), Mistral Medium 3.5 (128 B), and Qwen 3.8 (27 B). Muse Spark Open is a mixture of experts (MoE) model, which keeps only a fraction of its experts — and thus parameters — active, reducing compute at inference, and it is evaluated in NVFP4 precision. Mistral Medium 3.5 and Qwen 3.8 are dense architectures, where all parameters are active at inference, and they are evaluated in their native floating-point precision (FP8 and BF16, respectively).

Model

Total Parameters

Muse Spark Open

Our evaluation measures three metrics across a range of context sizes: time to first token (TTFT, in seconds), generation throughput (in tokens/second), and peak power usage (in watts). All the performance numbers in this post were obtained with mlx_lm.benchmark. For example, running Qwen 3.8 with 8,192 tokens of context and generating 128 tokens is performed with the command line:

mlx_lm.benchmark --model Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B -p 8192 -g 128 -b 1

A popular use of local LLMs on Mac Studio is running agentic experiences in a private environment, including agentic coding applications that often need large contexts. We therefore report performance at both 8,192 and 65,536 context sizes.

Raw TTFT and decode throughput are reported in Table 2 and Table 3, respectively.

Qwen 3.8 27B and Mistral Medium 3.5 128B fit comfortably on a single Mac Studio with 512GB, taking up to 68GB and 158GB of RAM in the large context size (65,536 tokens) setup. In Figure 2, we compare their inference performance on a single Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM, both on M3 Ultra and M5 Ultra.

Time to first token (TTFT) is essentially compute bound, and that is where the Neural Accelerators in the M5 Ultra GPU shine: the specialized hardware support for fast matrix-multiplication of the GPU Neural Accelerator directly translates into significant speedups for TTFT, up to 4.6× faster compared to an M3 Ultra (see Figure 2). That makes the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra the desktop of choice when it comes to handling tasks involving very large contexts.

Generation speed (in tokens per second) is memory-bandwidth bound. The M5 Ultra chip delivers 1.2 TB/s of unified memory bandwidth, up from 819 GB/s for the M3 Ultra. Here again, that translates directly into generation speed (see Figure 3), with the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra reporting 1.6× faster tokens/s.

TTFT Speedup

Single Mac Studio, M5 Ultra over an M3 Ultra baseline (1.0×)

Decode Speedup

Single Mac Studio, M5 Ultra over an M3 Ultra baseline (1.0×)

The Mac Studio is also energy-efficient for LLM inference (see Figure 4): peak power consumption is about 200W for the Mac Studio with M3 Ultra, and 300W for the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra — a fraction of the power used by a common toaster. More importantly, that modest amount of power consumption means a Mac Studio can be deployed for AI work in any home or office environment.

Peak Power Consumption

Context size of 65,536 tokens

While both the Qwen and Mistral models fit on a single Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM, Muse Spark Open would require more than 1.6TB of RAM in its native precision (BF16) for the model parameters alone. In a 4-bit quantized (NVFP4) format, the model memory footprint is lowered to about 493GB. Add the memory needed for intermediate computations during inference, and the model cannot fit on a single machine. It requires parallelization across multiple Mac Studio computers.

Very large frontier-class models like Muse Spark Open will not fit on a single machine. It is, however, possible to store half of the model on one Mac Studio and the other half on another. We can then pipeline the model’s inference across two computers: the first Mac Studio executes the first half of the model’s layers, then sends the output to the second Mac Studio, which executes the second half. This parallelization scheme is called pipeline parallelization (see Figure 5) and is extremely simple to implement, requiring only minimal code changes.

Splitting Large Models Across Multiple Computers

MLX supports different parallelization schemes, as described in the MLX distributed documentation. These rely on fast inter-machine communication: macOS 26.2 introduced a low-latency RDMA driver over Thunderbolt 5, and MLX (v0.30.1 and later) builds on top of this driver and provides new communication collectives (jaccl, pronounced “jackal”) for different parallelization schemes. In our setup, the two Mac Studios are connected with two Thunderbolt cables (to double the link bandwidth), providing the RDMA-over-Thunderbolt link that jaccl uses. Once the hosts are set up, MLX provides mlx.launch, a helper command to launch jobs across multiple nodes:

mlx.launch --hostfile hostfile.json --backend jaccl --env MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1 -- \
mlx_lm.benchmark --model mistralai/Mistral-Medium-3.5-128B -p 8192 -g 128 -b 1 --prefill-step-size 8192 --pipeline

In this command, --backend jaccl specifies the RDMA Thunderbolt driver backend. The --env MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1 flag enables an experimental MLX feature for fast CPU-GPU synchronization, reducing communication overhead between the CPU (which initiates the Thunderbolt communication) and the GPU (which does the compute).

In general, decode inference speed with pipeline parallelization (see Figure 7) is very similar to that of a single machine, since the layers are still evaluated sequentially. Communication overhead is also very low, as only the intermediate outputs between the two sets of layers need to be exchanged.

It is however notable that for very large contexts (65,536 tokens in our benchmark), pipeline parallelization ends up faster than a single node for prefill — up to ~1.8× faster (see Figure 6). This is because MLX segments large contexts into smaller chunks (here, 8,192 tokens, as set by --prefill-step-size 8192) and pipelines the prefill across the machines: while the second machine computes the later layers of chunk kkk, the first machine computes the earlier layers of chunk k+1k+1k+1, so consecutive chunks overlap in time. For even better compute parallelization, we next turn to tensor parallelization.

TTFT Speedup

Two Mac Studios with pipeline parallelization, over a single M5 Ultra baseline (1.0×)

Decode Speedup

Two Mac Studios with pipeline parallelization, over a single M5 Ultra baseline (1.0×)

Tensor parallelization (see Figure 5) distributes the LLM’s width across several computers, in contrast to pipeline parallelization, which distributes the model across its depth. Each machine now holds a fraction of each of the layers of the model, such that per-layer computation is parallelized. When efficiently implemented, tensor parallelization improves inference speed. However, tensor parallelization is more complex to implement than pipeline parallelization: each layer must be parallelized, which increases code complexity. The scheme also involves many small communication operations: for each input token and for each layer, one must broadcast inputs and aggregate outputs. As a result, a very low-latency communication technology like Thunderbolt RDMA, supported by MLX jaccl, is critical for this approach to yield any speedup.

With MLX’s high-level mlx.launch helper, it is easy to switch to tensor parallelization. The Mac Studio computers are connected in a Thunderbolt mesh, with each pair of machines linked peer-to-peer by two Thunderbolt cables. Assuming the hosts are set up, we simply launch the benchmark across multiple machines with:

mlx.launch --hostfile hostfile.json --backend jaccl --env MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1 -- \
mlx_lm.benchmark --model meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 -p 8192 -g 128 -b 1

Figure 8 and Figure 9 show the speedups obtained with two or four Mac Studio computers with M5 Ultra, relative to a single-machine baseline (or, for Muse Spark Open, the pipeline parallelization baseline). Notably, dense architectures scale better across multiple computers.

With a small number of machines, the communication overhead of tensor parallelization can offset some of its compute benefits at very large contexts, though this applies to prefill only. This shows up with Muse Spark Open, where separate normalization of the experts’ outputs adds some prefill communication, enough that at very large contexts (65,536 tokens), two-machine tensor parallelization lags behind two-machine pipeline parallelization. The approach however pays off as machines are added, as seen with four M5 Ultras. Decode is unaffected: Muse Spark Open sustains a significant decode speedup under tensor parallelization even at large contexts, comparable to dense models like Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5.

The two-cable mesh also pays off during prefill, where the extra link bandwidth is felt. For Muse Spark Open on four M5 Ultras at a 65,536-token context, two cables per link cut TTFT from about 50.5s (one cable) to 40.6s — the two-cable value reported in Table 2, the one-cable run being an additional experiment.

Recently, agentic AI on Mac has gained considerable traction, with agentic coding tools seeing widespread adoption among developers. With MLX, powering these tools locally is as simple as launching a server with the mlx_lm.server tool. For example, a server running Muse Spark Open on port 8080 is started with:

mlx.launch --hostfile hostfile.json --backend jaccl --env MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1 -- \
mlx_lm.server --model meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 --port 8080

As with mlx_lm.benchmark, the mlx_lm.server helper can be prefixed with mlx.launch to parallelize computation across multiple Mac Studios. From there, agentic AI can be enabled with tools like OpenCode, which can be easily configured to use that local LLM server:

{
"$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
"model": "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4",
"provider": {
"mlx": {
"npm": "@ai-sdk/openai-compatible",
"name": "Local MLX",
"options": {
"baseURL": "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1"
},
"models": {
"meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4": {
"name": "Muse Spark Open 816B (MLX)"
}
}
}
}
}

Many other local agentic AI experiences can be enabled through a similar approach.

Over the past year, we have worked on several key innovations in MLX to make it easier and more efficient to run state-of-the-art LLMs locally on recent Apple silicon. These include software support for the Neural Accelerators in the GPU of the M5 family of chips, low-latency communication across several Macs using RDMA over Thunderbolt, and efficient implementations of recent popular architectures such as mixture of experts (MoE). Each of these helps on its own, but it is their combination with the latest Apple silicon — Mac Studio with M5 Ultra, Neural Accelerators in the M5 Ultra GPU, 512GB of unified memory, and RDMA over Thunderbolt 5 — that now lets us run models like Muse Spark Open with more than 800B parameters locally, at up to 4.6× the start-up (time-to-first-token) speed of the previous generation of Mac Studio.
